impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that found Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments for headache and that the asserted claims were not invalid. This is a high-stakes ruling in the pharmaceutical patent space involving blockbuster migraine drug patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens pharmaceutical patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus claims for antibody-based therapies where the specification discloses methods of making and one specific embodiment, potentially broadening patent protection for biologic drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug manufacturers face greater difficulty in invalidating broad antibody method-of-treatment claims, potentially delaying market entry and increasing licensing costs.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive manufacturing and sales rights but retains the right to sue for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue third parties for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license for manufacturing and sales—retains sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. This clarifies the boundaries of patent licensing and standing doctrine.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure exclusive license agreements to retain litigation rights while granting broad commercial exclusivity, preserving their ability to enforce patents against infringers without joining the licensee.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a broader set of potential plaintiffs, as patent owners who have licensed away most commercial rights can still independently initiate infringement suits.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instruction and verdict form regarding patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and whether a single infringement question covering all asserted patents in the verdict form warranted a new trial.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement judgment involving building automation system wireless communication patents, ordering a new trial on infringement and damages due to flaws in the verdict form that used a single question for multiple patents. The court also remanded for further § 101 analysis on one patent while affirming eligibility of two others.
impacts.positiveImplications: Affirms that wireless communication innovations applied to building automation systems can survive § 101 challenges, supporting patent protection for IoT and smart building technologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders risk vacatur of jury verdicts where verdict forms bundle infringement questions across multiple patents into a single question, requiring more granular verdict forms that increase trial complexity.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a relay device for tracking farming operations by automatically capturing, processing, and sharing farming data are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in not finding the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that claims directed to automated farming data collection, processing, and sharing via a relay device attached to farming equipment were patent-ineligible under § 101, but vacated and remanded on the exceptionality determination for potential attorney's fees. The decision signals continued skepticism toward data-collection-and-processing patents in agricultural technology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in ag-tech and IoT data collection disputes gain support for invalidity defenses, and the remand on exceptionality signals that pursuing clearly ineligible patents may warrant fee-shifting.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology companies and other IoT innovators face heightened risk that patents claiming automated data capture, processing, and sharing systems will be invalidated under § 101.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting two invalidity grounds that were not included in its prior IPR petition but allegedly could have been discovered through a reasonably diligent search.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve on two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias on the other. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel by requiring more rigorous proof that prior art references were reasonably discoverable.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers retain broader ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after filing IPR petitions, as courts must more carefully evaluate whether prior art was truly discoverable before imposing estoppel.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a more difficult path to invoking IPR estoppel to streamline district court litigation, potentially increasing the number of invalidity theories they must defend against at trial.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim under the Defend Trade Secrets Act was time-barred where Insulet allegedly knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL and held that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred as a matter of law, finding that the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. This ruling underscores the strict three-year limitations period for federal trade secret claims and the importance of prompt enforcement action.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation can rely on the DTSA's strict three-year statute of limitations as a defense, providing certainty about exposure windows.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to know of misappropriation; delay beyond three years forecloses federal DTSA claims even where substantial damages are at stake.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert testimony and in its assessment of breach of contract damages arising from Ford's alleged misappropriation of vehicle configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury's award. The ruling affirms Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation of Versata's vehicle configuration software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the court's recognition that multiple damages models may be appropriate in trade secret cases, and the reinstatement of the breach of contract jury award supports enforceability of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacement software while licensing third-party software face sustained trade secret liability risk, and the remand for new damages analysis creates continued litigation exposure.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether the same analysis affected patent inventorship claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove its asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding that inventorship was improperly attributed based on contributions of generally known ideas. The counterfeiting claim was affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a stronger basis to challenge whether asserted secrets are truly protectable, particularly where the information is arguably generally known in the field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret claimants face a higher burden to demonstrate that their asserted secrets are not generally known, and interconnected patent inventorship claims may be undermined when trade secret protectability fails.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and properly struck damages theories for failure to adequately disclose them in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine issues of material fact precluded summary judgment on the extraterritoriality ground. The court affirmed other aspects of the lower court's ruling. This decision is part of the high-profile VLSI v. Intel patent litigation involving billions of dollars in potential damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against semiconductor and technology companies benefit from a narrower application of the extraterritoriality doctrine, preserving infringement claims where components or processes cross borders.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and design operations face broader exposure to domestic patent infringement claims even where significant activities occur overseas.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility determinations for some asserted patent claims while affirming eligibility for others, and affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages in this case involving digital communication standards used in televisions. The decision provides important guidance on § 101 eligibility for patents incorporated into industry communication standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Standards-essential patent holders in the communications space benefit from the court's affirmance of eligibility for certain constellation design patents and the denial of JMOL on damages, supporting enforcement of SEPs against major electronics manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement exposure, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty for some claims that must be re-evaluated.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether source code constitutes hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar (§ 102(b)), holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representatives may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that source code as computer commands is not hearsay. The decision clarifies important evidentiary standards for patent invalidity defenses based on prior sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded ability to use 30(b)(6) testimony and source code as evidence in invalidity challenges, even when the corporate witness lacks personal knowledge of historical events.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar invalidity challenges where prior art products were sold by third parties, as evidentiary hurdles for proving such sales are lowered.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it had previously filed and missed the deadline for seeking a stay of its original declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that a party cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action to restart the 30-day clock. This prevents gamesmanship in the interaction between ITC investigations and parallel district court patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate stay deadlines through strategic refiling of district court actions, preserving the ITC's role as a faster forum.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day mandatory stay deadline cannot reset it by refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate simultaneously in the ITC and district court at significant expense.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in a pharmaceutical composition patent refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the finding of no literal infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, holding that the pH claim limitation must be measured at the standard temperature used in the field. The court also affirmed that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents infringement. This ruling facilitates generic entry for Mylan's epoprostenol drug product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from the court's construction of pH limitations at standard field temperatures, providing a clear pathway for formulating non-infringing generic products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies with formulation patents containing pH-dependent claims may find their patent scope narrower than expected when pH is temperature-dependent.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to underlying patent litigation may file an IPR petition on the statutory deadline of a party to that litigation, effectively serving as a proxy petitioner, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant concerns about third-party proxy IPR petitions filed at the deadline of the real party in interest.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners gain protection from potentially deficient obviousness findings, and the case highlights judicial scrutiny of proxy IPR petitions that may circumvent statutory deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR proceedings to challenge competitor patents face uncertainty about the validity of proxy petitioner strategies and must ensure their obviousness arguments are fully developed.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when a patent owner is unable to locate a missing coinventor, and whether failure to name a coinventor renders the patents invalid.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents were invalid for omission of a coinventor where the patent owner acknowledged the coinventor's contributions but could not locate him to obtain consent for correction under § 256(a). The court held that § 256(b) judicial correction was not available on the facts presented, leaving the patents invalid.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers can assert inventorship defenses where patent owners failed to name all coinventors, providing a powerful invalidity tool even where the omission was unintentional.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with overseas manufacturers or contractors face significant patent validity risk if they fail to identify and maintain contact with all coinventors, as judicial correction may not be available.
